Corpulent means very fat or heavily overweight. When you describe a person as corpulent, you are saying that their body is noticeably large and heavy — carrying a significant amount of excess flesh. It goes well beyond "a little chubby." Think of a person with a big, rounded, heavy build — that is the image this word paints.

Corpulent does not describe someone who is slightly overweight or just a bit round. It describes someone who is substantially and visibly heavy. The word suggests a body that is thick, fleshy, and large in a way that is quite obvious. If someone is corpulent, you would notice it immediately just by looking at them.

It applies almost exclusively to people (and occasionally animals), not to objects.

This is where things get interesting for a learner.

Corpulent is a formal, literary word. It is not the kind of word you would casually throw into everyday conversation. It belongs more to books, formal writing, and careful speech. Because of this, it has a slightly old-fashioned or dignified feel to it — as if it belongs in a Victorian novel or a formal biography.

It is not a compliment, but it is also not quite the same as the blunt, harsh sting of calling someone "fat" to their face. Corpulent keeps a certain clinical or literary distance. That said, it is still quite direct — it does not soften the reality. Anyone described as corpulent would understand immediately that their size is being pointed out.

In short: it's the kind of word a narrator uses to describe a character in a novel, or a word a doctor might have used in a formal report a century ago — not something a friend says casually.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Since a learner needs to understand where a word "lives" among its neighbours, here is how corpulent relates to other words that describe body size:

  • Plump — mild and often almost affectionate. Barely negative, sometimes even charming. A plump grandma. This is much softer than corpulent.
  • Chubby — also mild, often used for children or in a fond way. Still far softer than corpulent.
  • Stout — a step up from chubby. Means solidly and heavily built, but not extreme. Sometimes used respectfully for someone who is thick and sturdy.
  • Portly — very close to corpulent. Often used for older, dignified men who carry a lot of weight. Slightly gentler in feel than corpulent.
  • Rotund — also close. Emphasises the roundness of a heavy body, often with a slightly humorous or affectionate quality.
  • Corpulent — formal, clearly heavy, no softening, no humour intended.
  • Obese — a cold, clinical, medical term. No emotion, strictly used in medical or scientific contexts.
  • Fat — the most direct and informal of all. In formal or literary writing, corpulent does the job that "fat" does in casual speech.

So on a scale from gentlest to bluntest: plump → chubby → stout → portly / rotund → corpulent → fat / obese.

Corpulent sits firmly on the heavier end of this scale, but with formality and literary dignity.
The antonyms of corpulent are words like slim, slender, lean, thin, slight, willowy, and svelte — all describing a person with little body fat and a light frame.

Reading a word in context is one of the best ways to truly absorb it. Here are several examples:

  • "The corpulent innkeeper waddled out from behind the counter to greet his guests."
  • "Despite his corpulent build, he moved with surprising grace on the dance floor."
  • "The portrait depicted a corpulent king draped in golden robes, seated on an enormous throne."
  • "Years of rich feasts had left the duke corpulent and short of breath."
  • "She described the villain as a corpulent, red-faced man who sweated constantly."

Notice that in every sentence, the word creates a vivid, clear picture of a very heavy person — and it fits naturally into formal or descriptive prose.

Corpulent is not a word you will hear every day. It is relatively rare in modern everyday speech. However, you will encounter it in classic literature, historical texts, formal essays, and sometimes in modern writing that is deliberately stylised or literary. Recognising it when you read it — and being able to use it correctly yourself — marks you as someone with a strong vocabulary.
If you need to remember just one thing: corpulent = very fat, used in a formal or literary way to describe a person with a large, heavy body.
